data.a-refusal-names-what-to-do-instead#A ref:
A rule here is not finished when it can say no. Every refusal names the program that does the same job properly: a GitHub write that must go through its own fleet command is refused and told which one, and a command line that records a status in a file is refused with the program that reports that status honestly.
A guard that only forbids teaches nothing and gets worked around. One that names the replacement moves the work onto the tool that cannot get it wrong.
data.an-escape-where-the-form-is-sometimes-ri:
Most rules carry one, as a single variable in front of one command:
GITSAFE_ALLOW_=1 It covers that command and nothing after it. The variable exists where the refused shape is sometimes legitimate — a throwaway repository under a volatile path, a backport deliberately started from an older base.
Some rules have none, deliberately. The rule added in v0.61.0 for a background command line that records its status in its output and exits with the status of the trailing echo refuses with no variable at all: the correct form already exists as a program, so an escape would only reopen the defect it was written for. Where the right way is already one command away, “allow it anyway” is not a missing feature.
data.judged-against-labelled-command-lines-no:
Two commands keep the guard honest, and both work on real command lines rather than on examples invented to pass:
hookcheck replays a corpus of labelled command lines — each one marked allow or deny — through the guard and reports how many it answers wrongly, in both directions. A false refusal counts exactly as much as a miss, because a guard that refuses correct work is one people route around. guardscan --rule replays a single rule over a body of command lines, which is how a new rule’s over-refusals are measured before it lands rather than discovered afterwards. A rule that reads shell text is also asked of the shells themselves: the oracle runs bash, dash and zsh, so what a grammar permits and what a production shell actually runs cannot quietly diverge. A runner missing one of those shells fails the oracle by name instead of reading as a pass.
data.the-bash-guard#The Bash guard:
guard-bash reads a command line before it runs and answers allow or deny. A harness that runs shell commands on an operator’s behalf calls it first, which makes it the most exercised command in the module: on a machine that has it wired in, every Bash call goes through it.
It is a guard on what a command does, not on who runs it. The rules exist because a written instruction is not a control — someone has to remember it at the moment they are busy doing something else.
data.why-this-page-does-not-list-the-rules#Wh:
For the same reason the API is not copied here: a hand-kept list of a moving thing becomes a second copy to go stale, and the first thing anyone would notice is that it disagrees with the tool.
The gitsafe README has one section per rule, each with the measurement that caused it — the command line that was really typed, what it really did, and what now refuses it.

data.checks#Checks: A check must have run, every check that ran must have passed, and GitHub must say the pull request is mergeable.
data.merge-gates#Merge gates: Every merge in the fleet goes through ghmerge (and ghrelease, which calls it). It merges on evidence, not on the absence of a failure.
data.quoting-a-reference-so-it-decides-nothin:
A reference inside a code span, a fenced block, an HTML comment or a plain URL is not a reference: that is how a body discusses an issue number without disposing of it, and it is the only honest way to name an issue that is already closed, since neither form fits one — Closes says this pull request finishes it, and Refs says it stays open on purpose.
Since v0.59.0 a code span may wrap a line break, as CommonMark allows. The earlier reading required a span to fit on one line, with two consequences that reflowing a paragraph to 80 columns could introduce invisibly: a quoted identifier became a real reference the author was asked to dispose of, and — the dangerous direction — a merely quoted Closes counted as a real disposition, so the gate could allow a merge on a decision GitHub itself never carries out.
A backtick run opens a span that only a run of the same length closes, and an unclosed run is literal text. The line breaks a span covered are preserved, because a keyword binds only within its own line.
⚠ A caller pinning an older gitsafe keeps the older reading: a body is judged by whichever version the tool that reads it was built with.
After the merge, every issue closed by keyword is read back. If GitHub did not close it (another repository, a base branch that is not the default, a missing permission) ghmerge closes it with the comment Closed by # (merge ). If it cannot, it exits 3 naming the issue.
The full rules are in the gitsafe README.
data.the-issues-gate#The issues gate:
A pull request must not land while an issue it mentions is left silently open. Before any write, ghmerge reads the pull request body and resolves each #N or owner/repo#N with one REST call. Each open issue must be preceded, on the same line, by:
a closing keyword (Closes, Fixes, Resolves and their other forms): the issue is closed by this pull request; or Refs: the issue stays open on purpose. A bare mention is refused, naming the issue and both forms. --issues-waiver "" merges anyway and records the reason as a comment on the pull request; there is no default and an empty reason is refused.
data.the-release-gate#The release gate:
A Go change in a tagged module must not be merged without a tag. Merged alone, the code is on main and invisible to go get: the module proxy resolves @latest to the highest release, and an untagged commit is only a pseudo-version (Go modules reference, “Versions” and “Mapping versions to commits”). It happened eight times, the last two on 2026-11-27.
The gate asks the question per module. Each changed file belongs to the module of the nearest go.mod above it, and a module’s releases are the tags under its own prefix:
Module Its tags the repository root vX.Y.Z a module in a subdirectory sub sub/vX.Y.Z a module in a major version subdirectory sub/v2 sub/v2.X.Y Tags of one module say nothing about another: a repository whose only tags are sub/v1.2.0 is a tagged module for sub and not for its root.
ghmerge refuses, before merging, a pull request that changes a non-test .go file, a go.mod or a go.sum (a rename out of one counts) in a module that has at least one stable release. It names the exact command, with the next PATCH over every tag of that module (GitHub’s tag listing is not in semver order):
ghmerge: merge AND tag it in one command: ghrelease owner/repo 42 sub/v0.10.1 ghrelease tags a prefixed module, one tag per merge, and checks the tag against the go.mod at the merge commit. A pull request that changes several tagged modules gets a command for each; the others run after the merge, and ghrelease tags the merge commit of an already merged pull request.
What the gate cannot read is not “no Go change”: a failed tag, file or tree read, a file list shorter than the pull request says, or a truncated tree (which cannot say which go.mod owns a file) refuses, naming the cause. --no-release "" merges anyway, for a series whose later pull request carries the tag; there is no default and an empty reason is refused. ghrelease passes it itself, since it is the release.
A module and its major version subdirectory that are both released (sub and sub/v2) share the prefix sub/: the gate names a version of the highest line, ghrelease rejects a wrong one against the go.mod, and --no-release is the way through.
The full rules are in the gitsafe README.

data.modules#Modules:
The 1 module of go-gitsafe. Each links to its source and to its generated API reference.
Module Reference gitsafe pkg.go.dev Descriptions live on the repositories themselves rather than being copied here, so there is one place to correct when one changes.

data.a-refusal-never-echoes-the-value#A refus: The refusal names the file, the kind of secret and the line, and points to the safe alternative. The value itself is never printed.
data.install#Install:
go install github.com/go-gitsafe/gitsafe/cmd/guard-read@v0.68.0 go install github.com/go-gitsafe/gitsafe/cmd/secretpeek@v0.68.0 Add the hook to ~/.claude/settings.json:
{"matcher":"Read|Bash","hooks":[{"type":"command","command":"~/.local/bin/guard-read","timeout":10}]}
data.it-fails-open-and-says-so#It fails open,:
A file it cannot read is allowed, with a line on stderr saying the content was not checked: a refusal is not a verdict about a file that was never seen. It does not cover ssh host cat file, a path built at run time, an interactive pager, or the Grep tool.
The gitsafe README has the full section.
data.secretpeek#secretpeek: It prints a file’s keys with each value replaced by its class, for example , so the structure is readable and the secret is not. With --key it prints one value, and only if that value is not a secret.
data.the-read-guard#The read guard: guard-read is a PreToolUse hook for the Read and Bash tools. It refuses a call that would display a file holding a credential, and it judges the file by its content, not by its name. secretpeek is the safe way to look at such a file instead. Both ship in gitsafe since v0.68.0.
data.what-it-scans#What it scans:
It opens regular files only, reads the first 1 MiB, and looks for:
JWTs and PEM private keys; GitHub, GitLab, AWS, Slack and Anthropic tokens; credentials embedded in a URL; password, secret or token keys with a value, in TOML, INI, YAML and JSON. Known credential directories are refused by path whatever the content. For the Bash tool it reads the file operands of programs that display content (cat, head, tail, grep, sed, awk, jq, strings, xxd, diff, and others) and < file redirects; globs are expanded, 64 files at most.
data.why-a-name-is-not-enough#Why a name is n: guard-bash has a name-based rule: it fires on a command substitution over a file called token, secret or .pem. A file called cli-config.toml does not look like a secret, and a plain cat on it can print an admin token straight into a transcript. The read guard opens the file and looks at what is in it.
